summary.text: A stable equilibrium is a balanced state where the system's potential energy sits at a local minimum.
If it is nudged slightly, the forces that result tend to restore the balance rather than push the system farther away.
Stability is an important property of mechanical equilibrium, and a balance is usually called stable only if it holds in all directions.

facts.label: Energy signature
facts.value: Potential energy at a local minimum

facts.label: Opposite case
facts.value: Unstable equilibrium sits at a local maximum of energy

facts.label: Higher dips
facts.value: Equilibria above the lowest energy are metastable states

facts.label: Gömböc
facts.value: A shape with just one stable and one unstable balance point

items.prompt: A marble rests at the bottom of a bowl. You nudge it slightly. What happens, and why?

options.label: It rolls away because it sits at an energy maximum
It stays wherever you put it, with no restoring force
It rolls back, because forces tend to restore the balance
It speeds off the bowl because nudges always grow

items.explain: At a local minimum of potential energy, a small disturbance produces forces that restore equilibrium.

items.prompt: A pencil is balanced on its sharp tip and then disturbed by the smallest nudge. Which equilibrium is this?

options.label: Stable, because it was balanced at first
Unstable, because forces push it farther away
Metastable, because it sits in a shallow dip
Neutral, because energy never changes

items.explain: At a local maximum of potential energy, a small displacement leads forces to move the system even farther from equilibrium.

items.prompt: A ball sits in a small dip on a hillside, with a deeper valley farther down. How is this equilibrium described?

options.label: Unstable, because it is on a hill
Neutral, because it is not the deepest point
Statically indeterminate, because the valley is deeper
Metastable, because its energy exceeds the lowest possible

items.explain: When several stable states exist, those with potential energy above the absolute minimum are metastable.

items.prompt: A ball in a saddle-shaped surface rolls back if pushed one way but rolls off if pushed another. Is its equilibrium called stable?

options.label: No, stable is used only when stable in all directions
Yes, because one direction is enough
Yes, because the average of the directions is zero
No, because saddles have no equilibrium at all

items.explain: Stability can differ by direction, and an equilibrium is generally called stable only if stable in all directions.

items.prompt: A paperweight sits on a desk. What kind of equilibrium is it?

options.label: Static equilibrium, a special case of mechanical equilibrium
Not in equilibrium, since it is touching the desk
Only equilibrium when it is moving at a constant speed
Unstable equilibrium by definition

items.explain: A stationary object is in static equilibrium, a special case of mechanical equilibrium; a paperweight on a desk is an example.

items.prompt: What marks a system as in mechanical equilibrium in terms of force?

options.label: The net force on each part is zero
The system must be completely motionless
The strongest force must point upward
The potential energy must be zero everywhere

items.explain: A particle is in mechanical equilibrium if the net force on it is zero, and a many-part system if the net force on each part is zero. Motion at constant velocity also counts.
